title: Check yourself: what overloads and overrides may declare

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: One class declares both `int parse(String s)` and `long parse(String s)`. What does this page say about that pair?

options.text: It is a valid overload: the two methods share one name
options.says: Key Aspects: sharing a name is not enough; overloaded methods must have different parameter lists.

options.text: It is not a valid overload: only the return types differ
options.says: Key Aspects: methods must have different parameter lists, and return type alone is not sufficient to distinguish overloaded methods.

options.text: It is an override: the second method replaces the first
options.says: Common Pitfalls: overriding redefines a method in a subclass, while these two methods sit in the same class.

questions.stem: A subclass means to replace `makeSound()` but spells it `makeSond()`, with `@Override` above it. What does this page say happens?

options.text: The compiler reports an error before anything runs
options.says: Q5: if @Override sits on a method that does not override one, the compiler generates an error, catching typos in names early.

options.text: The JVM throws an exception when the call is made
options.says: The page says the mistake is caught at compile time, not at run time.

options.text: The program runs and the parent's version is used
options.says: That is what happens without the annotation; with it, the page says the compiler rejects the misspelt method.

concepts: The return type alone cannot distinguish two overloads.
@Override makes the compiler reject a method that does not actually override one.
